clinician.trajectory_summary: A 61-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of fever and progressive headache, accompanied by bilateral leg weakness and paraesthesias. Physical examination revealed slight neck stiffness. Initial workup demonstrated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) moderate pleocytosis (140 leucocytes/μL) with mononuclear cell dominance consistent with viral meningoencephalitis. Brain MRI revealed characteristic rhombencephalitis findings with T2-weighted hyperintensity involving the tegmentum pontis and cerebellar vermis, and FLAIR hyperintensity with swelling of the entire cerebellar vermis. The combination of lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis, brainstem/cerebellar inflammation on neuroimaging, and the myelitic presentation (bilateral lower extremity weakness) constitutes the classic triad for the meningoencephalomyelitic form of tick-borne encephalitis.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: CSF demonstrates moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis (140 cells/μL) with mononuclear dominance consistent with viral CNS infection
MRI reveals T2 hyperintense lesions in the tegmentum pontis and cerebellar vermis indicating rhombencephalitis
FLAIR imaging shows hyperintensity and swelling of the entire cerebellar vermis with minimal paravermis involvement, confirming posterior fossa inflammation
Clinical presentation of subacute fever, headache, neck stiffness, and bilateral lower extremity weakness/paraesthesias is consistent with TBEV meningoencephalomyelitis

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: CSF shows mononuclear cell dominance rather than neutrophilic predominance typical of bacterial infection; no documented positive blood cultures
MRI shows pontine/cerebellar involvement rather than the typical temporal lobe/limbic system involvement seen in HSV encephalitis; no HSV PCR documentation available
Acute febrile presentation with CSF pleocytosis favors infectious etiology; no documentation of autoimmune antibodies
